title: How the solvent changes the rate
asks: A reaction is run in two solvents. Say which is faster and why, in terms of how the solvent treats the starting materials and the transition state.

know.h: The rate is set by {{Ea}}, the gap between the starting materials and the transition state. A solvent changes the rate only when it stabilizes one of these two more than the other.
Solvation is stabilization. Polar solvent molecules surround a charge and lower its energy. The more charge a species has, and the more concentrated it is, the more a polar solvent stabilizes it.

The method: write the charges on the starting materials, sketch the transition state with its partial charges, and compare. More charge in the transition state than at the start: a more polar solvent is faster. Less charge (or the same charge spread out): a more polar solvent is slower.

Lecture case 1, neutral to charged. Triethylamine and iodoethane are neutral. The transition state has δ+ on N and δ- on I. The more polar solvent (50:50 {{H2O}}:ethanol against 25:75) stabilizes the transition state more than the starting materials, lowers {{Ea}}, and is faster. [[rxn:CCN(CC)CC + CCI>>CC[N+](CC)(CC)CC.[I-]]]

Lecture case 2, charged to neutral. {{HO-}} and {{(CH3)3S+}} are both fully charged and well solvated. In the transition state [HOδ-···{{CH3}}···Sδ+] the charge is being destroyed. The more polar solvent stabilizes the starting materials more than the transition state, raises {{Ea}}, and is slower. [[rxn:[OH-] + C[S+](C)C>>CO + CSC]]

{{SN1}}: increase the polarity of the solvent and the rate goes up. The substrate is neutral, and the transition state of the rate-determining step has δ+ on carbon and δ- on the leaving group, so a polar solvent stabilizes it more than the starting compound.

Solvent types. Polar protic solvents are hydrogen-bond donors: water, methanol, ethanol, acetic acid. Polar aprotic solvents have no O-H or N-H: DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile. Hexane and pentane are nonpolar.
In a water and ethanol mixture, more water means a more polar solvent.

Anionic nucleophiles. A protic solvent hydrogen-bonds to an anion and holds it in a cage. That lowers the energy of the starting nucleophile more than it lowers the transition state, where the charge is spread over two atoms, so {{SN2}} is slower. A polar aprotic solvent dissolves the salt but cannot hydrogen-bond to the anion, so the nucleophile is free and {{SN2}} is faster.
know.from: Lecture 11/10, p. 5 and flowchart (polar protic solvates negative ions); standard

know.h: The course summary: {{SN2}} is favoured by a polar aprotic solvent, {{SN1}} and {{E1}} by a polar protic solvent.
A polar solvent stabilizes both the starting materials and the transition state when both carry charge. The answer is about which is stabilized more.
Be able to sketch the two energy curves: for case 1 the top of the hill drops in the more polar solvent, for case 2 the starting level drops more than the top.

method: Write the charge on each starting material: neutral, a full plus or a full minus.
Sketch the transition state of the rate-determining step and put the partial charges on it.
Decide what happens to charge on the way up: created, destroyed, or spread over more atoms.
Decide which the more polar solvent stabilizes more, the starting materials or the transition state.
Turn that into the barrier: transition state stabilized more means a lower Ea and a faster reaction, starting materials stabilized more means a higher Ea and a slower reaction.
If the nucleophile is an anion, also ask whether the solvent is protic (hydrogen bonds hold the anion back) or aprotic (the anion is free).

pitfalls.h: Saying that a more polar solvent always makes a reaction faster. It depends on where the charge is.
Comparing the starting materials with the products. The rate depends on the transition state.
Calling acetone, DMSO or DMF protic because they are polar. Protic means an O-H or N-H that can donate a hydrogen bond.
Saying a polar solvent destabilizes the transition state. It stabilizes both levels, one more than the other.
Choosing a protic solvent for an {{SN2}} reaction with an anionic nucleophile because the salt dissolves well in it.
